Tax offices in Jackson and Raymond

Two county seats, Jackson and Raymond, split Hinds County into a First Judicial District (Jackson) and a Second Judicial District (Raymond). The tax collector, tax assessor and chancery clerk all keep an office in each. Property tax here involves three elected offices. Value comes from the assessor. Bills and payments go through the collector. Deeds, the appeal hearing process before the Board of Supervisors and delinquent tax collection belong to the chancery clerk. Doors open at 8:00 a.m. and close at 5:00 p.m., weekdays, with legal holidays off.

OfficeJackson (First District)Raymond (Second District)
Tax Collector316 S. President St., 601-968-6587127 W. Main St., 601-857-5574
Tax AssessorMail: P.O. Box 22908, 601-968-6616Mail: P.O. Box 549, 601-857-8787
Chancery Clerk316 S. President St., 601-968-6508Main St. Annex Building, 601-857-8055

Call before you drive, since numbers and hours can change. Each office has a page on the county site: Tax Collector, Tax Assessor and Chancery Clerk.

How the assessor values a house

Every year the assessor compiles the taxable parcels, values them, applies the state ratio and certifies the roll for the Board of Supervisors. Parcel counts range from about 100 in Learned to more than 70,000 inside Jackson, for a county total above 106,000.

A Class I property, meaning a single-family home its owner lives in, is assessed at 10 percent of true value. A rental house or other real estate is Class II at 15 percent. Multiply true value by the ratio and then by millage to get the tax.

One quarter of taxable property is reviewed each year, so all of it is seen at least every four years. For a typical house, that means an appraiser driving by and comparing the house to the drawings and field sheet on file. You hear from the assessor only if the appraiser sees a difference from the file, and nobody has to enter your home. Sales ratio studies compare appraised values with real sale prices.

  • Deeds on file with the chancery clerk decide who the owner is as of January 1.
  • The roll reaches the Board of Supervisors on the first Monday in July.

Dates on the Hinds County tax calendar

Money is due February 1 for the year before. Land on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday and you get until the following Monday without a penalty. Mailed statements go out each December, and paying in three installments is allowed for current taxes.

Think of the year as a sequence. Ownership is frozen on January 1, and homestead filings run until April 1. The Board of Supervisors gets the roll in early July, protests close in early August, and bills follow in November and December. Anything still unpaid after the deadline heads to the sale at the end of August.

Late tax grows by one-half of one percent each month, with a part month counted whole. The governor can push the due date back during unusual conditions, by proclamation, for as long as 60 days at a time.

How to appeal your assessment

To get a hearing, go through the Chancery Clerk. The Board of Supervisors hears appeals, and the request usually has to be in by the first Monday in August.

Do not wait for August. An owner can sit down with the assessor about values at any time of year, and Mississippi Code 27-35-89 covers the formal appeal after that. Business personal property works differently: values are posted after the first Monday in July, review runs through July 31, and a formal protest has to reach the chancery clerk by 9:00 a.m. on that first Monday in August.

Evidence wins. Your own recent appraisal is the best exhibit, since the board looks at how fair and accurate the value is. A wrong square footage on the file can sometimes bring a refund for earlier years through the chancery clerk.

When taxes go unpaid

Property that is still delinquent is offered at the August tax sale, on the last Monday of the month. A parcel with no bid is struck off to the state. The chancery clerk collects the delinquent amounts, and older years come ahead of the current one.

On a delinquent account the clerk allows no installments and takes only cash or a money order. Two years after the sale, redemption ends. Then the property goes to the state or the buyer gets a tax deed, and the former owner has lost the house.

For property sold to the state, call the Secretary of State at 1-866-835-2637. Delinquent and tax sale lists are posted on the county site.

  • Redeeming means paying the delinquent taxes with statutory damages and interest.
  • Selling before the sale date lets you clear the taxes from the proceeds.
  • Waiting until after the sale still leaves redemption open, but only through the chancery clerk.

Selling with taxes owed

Nothing stops you from selling while taxes are unpaid, since closing clears them. A title search reveals back taxes, mortgages and any other liens, and the total is usually taken from your proceeds at the table.

Have the search done before any money changes hands, by an attorney or title company, because the chancery clerk's office may not search records or prepare a deed. A valid deed carries the seller's notarized signature, a legal description with indexing instructions, and the names, addresses and phone numbers of sellers, buyers and the preparer.

A buyer who occupies the home before January 1 can apply for homestead exemption from January 1 to April 1, which lowers that year's tax. Selling for cash leaves the order of steps alone, since recording and tax still come first. It only removes the wait on a buyer's lender.

Older homes, inherited houses and rentals are common here. Probate and heirship questions belong to the chancery court, and the clerk files the papers. When the owner has died, title may need clearing before anyone can sign a deed.

What to do first when you decide to sell

Dig out the parcel number printed on your last statement. One call to the collector, in either city, shows this year's bill and whether any older year is still open. An older delinquent year gets paid first, and only cash or a money order is accepted for it.

After that, find out how the assessor describes your house. A wrong square footage is a common error, and correcting it before listing can lower a buyer's future bill. Hand the deed details to your title company or attorney so any lien shows up early. At closing the payoff comes out of your proceeds and the deed goes to the chancery clerk, which decides who is owner of record on the next January 1.

A quick cash sale follows the same path without a lender, so timing depends mostly on how fast the title search returns.

Paying your bill

The Tax Collector accepts cash, check or credit card with a 2.25 percent surcharge. Tags paid by personal check are held for 10 working days. Offices are at 316 S. President St. in Jackson and 127 W. Main St. in Raymond. Whichever you use, bring the statement or parcel number so staff can find the right account quickly.

The county and its housing market

Hinds County is in central Mississippi and is the state's most populous county, with 227,742 residents at the 2020 census. It covers 877 square miles. The cities are Byram, Clinton, Jackson and Raymond. The towns are Bolton, Edwards, Learned, Terry and Utica. Part of Jackson lies in Madison and Rankin counties, so check which county bills a given parcel.

Public schools are served by three districts: Jackson Public School District, Clinton Public School District and Hinds County School District. Population has been falling, from 250,998 in 1980 to 227,742 in 2020, with an estimate of 211,888 for 2025. That trend can mean fewer buyers per listing, and a clean tax record removes one obstacle to closing.

Frequently asked questions

What is the payment deadline for Hinds County property tax?

The deadline is February 1 for last year's assessment, moving to the next Monday if it is a weekend or holiday. After that, interest builds at one-half of one percent monthly.

Which offices take a property tax payment in Hinds County?

The Tax Collector, at 316 S. President St. in Jackson or 127 W. Main St. in Raymond. Cards carry a 2.25 percent surcharge, and cash and checks are taken as well.

What share of a home's value is taxed in Hinds County?

Ten percent of true value for a single-family home the owner lives in, and 15 percent for other real property like a rental. Combined county, city and school millage then applies to that figure.

How late can I file an appeal of my Hinds County valuation?

The first Monday in August in most cases. Ask the Chancery Clerk for a Board of Supervisors hearing, and talk to the assessor long before that date.

Is it possible to sell in Hinds County with delinquent taxes?

It is. At closing the title company deducts what is owed from your proceeds. If a tax sale has already taken place, redemption is paid through the chancery clerk within two years.

Assessor and Collector offices in Hernando

DeSoto County property tax involves two desks at the same Hernando address. In Suite 100 of 365 Losher Street the Tax Assessor (662-469-8029) puts a value on every parcel. In Suite 110 the Tax Collector (662-469-8030) issues the bill and receives payment. A second collection counter operates on BJ Chain Drive in Olive Branch, handy if you live in the north end.

Mississippi requires a new valuation of real property at least every four years and of taxable personal property annually. The assessor does not have to go inside your home. Rates are not on a ballot for you. Each of the county, your city and the school district decides how much money it needs, and local officials combine that into the millage that lands on your statement.

Mississippi property classes and assessment ratios
ClassWhat it coversAssessment ratio
Class ISingle-family, owner-occupied home10%
Class IIOther real property, such as rentals and land15%
Class IIIBusiness personal property15%
Class IVPublic utility property30%
Class VMotor vehicles30%

Multiply true value by the class ratio, then by millage, and you have the tax. Because a rented house falls in Class II, a larger fraction of its value is taxed than for a home its owner lives in.

When the money is due

Whoever holds title on January 1 is the person assessed. Statements show up in November and December, with February 1 as the payment date. Should that date fall on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, paying on the Monday after carries no penalty or interest.

Real estate left unpaid can be offered at the county tax sale. The calendar differs by county, with some picking the first Monday in April and others the last Monday in August. Phone the collector to learn which applies in DeSoto.

  • A winning bidder at that sale gets no instant clean title, since the former owner keeps two years from the sale to redeem (Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3).
  • With no bidder, the parcel goes to the State of Mississippi, and the Secretary of State handles it at 1-866-835-2637.
  • Unpaid tax clouds the title, so a title company will want it cleared when you close.

Appealing a valuation

Your route runs through the Chancery Clerk, who arranges a hearing in front of the county Board of Supervisors. Put the request in by the first Monday in August, which lands ahead of the tax due date.

Before you file, talk to the assessor and carry comparable sales or repair bids. A cracked foundation or an aging roof is far easier to prove with photographs and a contractor's quote than with argument. The board checks valuations, listens to objections and then adopts the rolls, so the August date does not bend.

Homestead exemption

Homestead trims the bill for the person living in the house, and it stays with that owner rather than the property. The window to apply at the Tax Assessor is January 1 through April 1. Unless ownership or marital status changes, the filing carries forward and you skip the yearly paperwork.

For an owner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled and otherwise eligible, the first $75,000 of true value is exempt from tax. Two things block it: the owner or spouse being out of compliance with state income tax laws, and a vehicle tagged outside the home county. Buyers who intend to live in the house should apply in their first year, because after April 1 the benefit waits for the next assessment year.

Selling with taxes owed

A tax balance seldom blocks a sale. Your title company gets the payoff from the collector and deducts it before handing you your check. When the parcel was already sold at a tax sale, the redemption sum is deducted as well.

Watch for these local snags:

  • Confirm that the name, mailing address and homestead status on the roll are current. A statement mailed to an old address is still owed.
  • An inherited house may carry unpaid tax or paperwork never recorded, and both must be fixed before the deed can move.
  • A tenant-occupied rental sits in Class II, with the higher ratio, which an investor buyer will notice.
  • A newer subdivision may be inside a city levy while a house outside the limits is not, so similar homes can see different bills.

Selling for cash trims some of that, since the buyer takes the house as is and the closing date is yours to pick. The title still has to be clean, any mortgage paid off and the current year's tax settled on the closing statement.

A quick way to find your balance

Use the county's online tax search first. It lets you look up real and personal property by name, parcel or address and shows what is due. A phone call to the collector then catches items that print separately, such as tax-sale and earlier-year amounts.

  1. Pull the parcel number off your deed or the assessor's lookup.
  2. Ask the Tax Collector, in Hernando or Olive Branch, for the current and earlier-year figures.
  3. Check with the Chancery Clerk to see whether a sale was ever held on the parcel.
  4. Pass every number to the title company so it can settle taxes at closing.

Where DeSoto County sits

The county occupies the far northwest of Mississippi, just south of Shelby County, Tennessee, with Hernando as seat. Four cities hold most residents: Hernando, Horn Lake, Olive Branch and Southaven. Walls is a town, and places such as Lake View, Lynchburg and Pleasant Hill are census-designated. Lake Cormorant, Nesbit and Cockrum are unincorporated.

Your parcel's tax district settles whether a city or school levy applies, so check that before pricing a sale. The 2020 census counted 185,314 people, and the 2025 estimate is 197,918. One school system, the DeSoto County School District, covers everyone, and the largest in the state, although attendance zones vary by address.

Housing stock and commuting

The county farmed cotton first, then dairy and soybeans, before subdivisions replaced the fields. Homes in Southaven went on sale in 1958, and Interstate 55 opened through Hernando in 1964. The population was 67,910 in 1990 and reached 161,252 by 2010. Houses here span several building eras: a 1970s ranch in Horn Lake and a 2010s two-story in Olive Branch face different repair lists, even though the same collector bills both.

Interstate 55, Interstate 69, Interstate 269, U.S. 51 and U.S. 61 carry most traffic. The county has no fixed-route transit of its own, so most households depend on a car.

Frequently asked questions

When are DeSoto County property taxes due?

February 1, covering property assessed the year before. If that day is a weekend or holiday, the following Monday still counts with no penalty.

Where do I pay property tax in DeSoto County?

Bring it to the Tax Collector at 365 Losher Street, Suite 110, Hernando, or the Olive Branch branch. The Hernando number is 662-469-8030, and it is smart to confirm hours and payment types first.

How do I appeal my DeSoto County assessment?

Ask the Chancery Clerk to put you before the Board of Supervisors. File by the first Monday in August, before the tax comes due.

Can I sell a DeSoto County house with taxes owed?

Yes, and it happens often. The title company collects the payoff figure and pays the county from your sale proceeds. A parcel sold at a tax sale also has to have its redemption amount paid.

Does DeSoto County have one school district?

Yes, a single countywide district, and it is the largest in Mississippi. Ask the district which attendance zone covers a specific address.

Lowndes County overview

Columbus is the seat and the only city of Lowndes County, which hugs the Alabama line on Mississippi's eastern side. The count was 58,879 people in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 57,346, a decline of 2.6 percent. Housing demand is steady rather than booming, tied to manufacturing, Columbus Air Force Base and the Mississippi University for Women.

Two public school systems serve the county, the Columbus Municipal School District and the Lowndes County School District, and the tax bill depends partly on which one covers your address. Each taxing body picks its own levy, and the sum becomes your millage rate. Towns such as Caledonia, Artesia and Crawford, plus rural areas to the west, make up the rest of the market for sellers.

The Lowndes County Tax Office

The Tax Office is at 1121 Main Street in Columbus, MS 39701. Call 662-329-5700 to reach the tax collector, or 662-329-3940 for the assessor's mapping line. The county's own site is lowndescountyms.com. Search results for a similarly named county in another state can show a different due date, so stay on that address.

TaskWhere to do it
Pay property tax or car tagsTax Office counter, or the county's online portal at lowndes.ibcpayments.com
Look up a parcel and its tax statusProperty Link real property search, run by Delta Computer Systems
Check a parcel map or boundaryAssessor's mapping line, 662-329-3940, or the appraisal maps from Tri-State Consulting Services

A parcel lookup is the best first step before you talk to any buyer: the record shows the assessed value, the ratio applied and whether any year is open. The Tax Office page has the current office hours, so look there or call before you drive in.

When Lowndes County property taxes are due

The bill covers the prior year's assessment and must be paid on or before February 1. Should that day be a weekend or legal holiday, Monday becomes the last penalty-free day. Ownership is fixed on January 1, and the statement shows up in the mail around November or December.

  • January 1 to April 1: window to apply for homestead exemption.
  • First Monday in August: usual deadline to appeal with the Board of Supervisors.
  • February 1: payment due.
  • Past February 1: one-half of one percent interest each month.

If you are listing in the fall, ask the buyer's side early who is taking the bill that arrives in November or December. The usual approach is to split the bill by closing date, and the split belongs in writing in the contract or on the settlement statement.

Appealing your assessment

If the value looks wrong, ask the Chancery Clerk to put you on the Board of Supervisors' hearing list. Plan to do it by the first Monday in August, ahead of the due date.

Real property in Mississippi has to be revalued at least once every four years, so your number can move when your parcel comes up. Interior inspections of houses are not required, and the assessor values every structure on a parcel, outbuildings included. If your house was recorded at the wrong size, a refund for earlier years may be possible through the Chancery Clerk.

Before you file, ask the assessor's staff to walk you through the value on the roll. Bring photos, any recent appraisal and recent sales of similar houses.

Homestead exemption

Homestead exemption covers the house you live in. Take the application to the assessor in the county where the house stands before April 1, and not earlier than January 1. It carries over from year to year, but you should file again if your marital status or ownership changes.

An owner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled, and who meets the other tests can shield the first $75,000 of true value. Proof of disability may include a VA release form, a Social Security benefit report or letters from two physicians. Falling behind on state income tax filings, for you or a spouse, can cost you eligibility, and so can registering a vehicle in a different county.

An inherited house that no one lives in gets no homestead, so expect the 15 percent ratio on it rather than 10.

What happens to unpaid taxes?

Land with unpaid taxes is offered at the county tax sale, and the former owner keeps a two-year right to buy it back. A redeeming owner pays the delinquent taxes, the buyer's money comes back with monthly interest, and if two years pass with no redemption the buyer can get a tax deed from the chancery clerk. The county has run its sale online through GovEase.

The statutes put these auctions on either the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August. Which one applies this year is a question for the Tax Office. For land already sold to the state, call the Secretary of State at 1-866-835-2637.

If you are behind, selling ahead of the auction date is the easy way out, because the title company settles the taxes from what you receive. If the auction has already happened, the redemption amount is the figure to get, and the Chancery Clerk or the Tax Office can supply it. Keep the paperwork from any payment, because a buyer's title company will ask to see it.

Selling a Lowndes County house

A sale here follows the usual Mississippi steps: title search, a prepared deed, payment of taxes and liens at closing, and recording with the chancery clerk.

  1. Pull the parcel on the Property Link search and read the assessed value and tax status.
  2. Get a payoff number from the Tax Office for each year that is past due.
  3. Confirm whether homestead is on file. It is the difference between a 10 percent ratio on a home you occupy and 15 percent on everything else.
  4. For an inherited house, the chancery court handles probate and the clerk files the papers.
  5. Pick an attorney or title company early so the deed and closing are ready.

Owners in Columbus, Caledonia, New Hope and the rural west sometimes sell as-is because of repairs, a move for work or an estate. A cash buyer closes without a bank appraisal or a lender's repair list. Cash Home Buyers reviews every Lowndes County house on its own facts, and we name no price or closing date until we have seen the details.

Bring your deed, a recent tax receipt and any mortgage payoff statement to the first conversation with a title company. Those three papers settle most early questions about who holds title, what is owed and which county office has to sign off on the numbers. Heirs should add the probate paperwork, and landlords should add any lease that is still running.

Frequently asked questions

When are Lowndes County, MS property taxes due?

The deadline is February 1. A Saturday, Sunday or holiday deadline rolls to Monday, and any bill paid after that picks up one-half of one percent a month.

Where is the Lowndes County Tax Office?

It is at 1121 Main Street in Columbus, MS 39701, phone 662-329-5700. An online county portal takes real property tax, personal property tax and car tag payments.

What is the Lowndes County appeal deadline?

Usually the first Monday in August. Contact the Chancery Clerk to get a hearing in front of the Board of Supervisors.

How do I confirm I am on the right county website?

Use lowndescountyms.com, the Mississippi county's site. A similarly named site for a county in another state lists a different due date.

Can I sell my Lowndes County house if taxes are overdue?

Yes. The title company pays back taxes from your proceeds at closing. A parcel the county has already auctioned stays redeemable for two years from the auction date.

Assessor and Collector offices

Harrison County runs its tax work out of both judicial districts. The Tax Assessor values property and the Tax Collector bills it, and the assessor's office is responsible for more than 100,000 parcels of real and personal property.

  • Assessor, Gulfport: 1801 23rd Avenue, phone 228-865-4043.

How value becomes a tax bill

The assessor sets true value, the state ratio for the property class gives the assessed value, and the millage rate finishes the job. The assessor has no hand in the millage. It comes from the taxing agencies: the cities, the schools and the County Board of Supervisors.

ClassPropertyRatio of value

For Class I and II property, the county site quotes Mississippi Appraisal Manual language saying true value rests on current use, regardless of location. A beachfront owner should not count on the water view to drive the assessment.

Tax calendar and late charges

The Collector mails statements December 1. Payment is due by February 1, and interest of one half of one percent per month begins February 2. The rest of the cycle looks like this:

  1. The collector honors the postmark when figuring monthly interest on mailed payments.
  2. Delinquent real property is published in the newspaper in July, and no partial payments are accepted after that.
  3. The tax sale is held on the last Monday in August, and payment must arrive by 5:00 p.m. the Friday before.
  4. Parcels sold can be redeemed through the Chancery Clerk, normally opening by October 1.
  5. Personal property taxes unpaid on September 30 go to an attorney, adding 20% of the total due.
  6. Mobile home taxes go out January 1 and are due February 1.

The sale list goes to GovEase, and a parcel is not pulled once it has been handed over. Only certified funds work to take part in the sale, and the office warns against mailing a check the week before it. If the August date is close, pay by phone at 228-865-4040, option 3, instead of trusting the mail.

After a tax sale: redemption

Two years after the sale date, the owner can still buy the parcel back (Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3). The Chancery Clerk is required to tell the owner about the sale and the right to redeem.

Two things follow for a seller. First, a house that already went through a sale cannot close until redemption is paid. Second, land with no buyer passes to the State, and the Secretary of State manages it at 1-866-835-2637. Do not wait for either to happen: clear the balance well ahead of August.

How to appeal your assessment

To appeal, ask the Board of Supervisors for a hearing and work through the Chancery Clerk. File by the first Monday in August, ahead of the due date.

Begin by calling the assessor in Gulfport or Biloxi with repair bids or a recent appraisal. No interior inspection is required, so your house may be valued on its exterior alone. If the record misstates square footage, ask about a correction and a possible refund for earlier years through the Chancery Clerk.

Homestead exemption

Whether the next owner claims homestead changes their bill, so raise it before closing. The Tax Assessor takes applications January 1 through April 1, and a filing stays good unless circumstances change.

For an owner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled and otherwise eligible, the first $75,000 of true value is exempt. Service members stationed outside Mississippi can qualify if they claim Mississippi residency and follow state law, and both spouses must qualify. Ask the assessor what proof to bring.

Selling with taxes owed

Watch for these before you list or accept a cash offer:

  • An unpaid balance close to the August sale. The Friday deadline is firm.
  • Damage or repairs left from a storm, which can block a conventional buyer's loan.
  • A mobile home that was moved or destroyed but still appears on the roll. You must tell the Tax Assessor, with proof, to remove it.
  • Inherited houses where taxes lapsed while the family sorted out ownership.

A cash buyer purchases as-is, so repairs do not delay closing, but liens, taxes and title issues still must be cleared. Ask the Collector for the payoff and give it to the title company so it comes out of your proceeds. Confirm every date and amount with the county office.

Storm history and housing

Two hurricanes define the building history: Camille on August 17, 1969, and Katrina on August 29, 2005, both with catastrophic damage. Hurricane Georges in 1998 also pushed the Tchoutacabouffa River over its banks near Old Highway 67 and Mississippi 15.

Buyers ask the same questions first. Is the lot in a flood zone, was the house rebuilt after a storm, and is the roof recent? Ask your insurer and the county for the facts on your own parcel. The French built Fort Maurepas in 1699, hotels opened along the coast in the 1880s and Keesler Field arrived in the early to mid 1900s, which is why a Biloxi bungalow, a Long Beach cottage and a newer D'Iberville subdivision can have so little in common.

Harrison County in brief

Harrison County has two county seats, Gulfport and Biloxi, and the assessor keeps a separate office in each judicial district. It was established on February 5, 1841, from parts of Hancock, Jackson and Perry counties. The 2024 population estimate is 217,136. The cities are Biloxi, D'Iberville, Gulfport, Long Beach and Pass Christian, and the school districts are Biloxi, Gulfport, Harrison County, Long Beach and Pass Christian.

Total area is 976 square miles, 402 of them (41%) water, which makes it the second-largest county in Mississippi by total area. Gulfport is the state's chief port, with a ship channel to the Gulf of Mexico.

February 1. Interest of 0.5% a month starts February 2. Bills go out December 1, and the postmark decides whether a mailed payment is on time.

When is the Harrison County tax sale?

It falls on the last Monday in August. Pay real property taxes by 5:00 p.m. the Friday before, since the list goes to GovEase and parcels are not pulled afterward.

Where do I pay property taxes in Harrison County?

Pay at the Gulfport, Biloxi or Multi-Services Building office, through the county's online payment link, by phone at 228-865-4040 option 3, or at a kiosk in D'Iberville, Long Beach or Pass Christian.

Can I redeem a Harrison County parcel after the tax sale?

Yes, within two years of the sale (Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3). Redemption runs through the Chancery Clerk, which normally opens it by October 1 after a sale.

How do I appeal my Harrison County assessment?

Ask the Chancery Clerk for a Board of Supervisors hearing. The normal cutoff is the first Monday in August, before the tax comes due.

Jackson County at a glance

Down in Mississippi's southeastern corner, Jackson County borders the Gulf of Mexico about 190 miles from the state capital. It has no connection to the city of Jackson, which is in Hinds County. The county seat is Pascagoula, and the other cities are Gautier, Moss Point and Ocean Springs. Vancleave, Escatawpa, Gulf Park Estates and Latimer are among the unincorporated communities.

The population was 143,252 in 2020 and is estimated at 147,666 for 2025, up from 118,015 in 1980. The county is heavily industrial, with shipbuilding, refinery and manufacturing jobs around Pascagoula, Moss Point and Ocean Springs. Steady employment like that brings buyers who want to live close to work. Storm-exposed and older houses tend to sit longer on the market.

Interstate 10 and US 90 run east and west through the county, and state highways 57, 63 and 609 run north. Much of the county is water or protected land, so a lot of the housing is packed along the coast and the main roads.

Tax assessor and tax collector offices

Jackson County is one of 17 Mississippi counties that keep the tax assessor and the tax collector as separate offices. A sale touches both desks. The assessor owns the value and the exemptions, while the collector owns the bill and the payment.

OfficeWhat it handlesContact

Both offices have pages on the county website: Tax Collector and Tax Assessor. Parts of those pages load slowly, so call before you drive over. Ask the same call whether the collector has a drop box if you would rather not wait in line.

Property tax calendar

Whoever holds title on January 1 is the owner of record for that year's bill. Statements are mailed in November or December, and the payment deadline is February 1. When that date falls on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, Monday is the effective cutoff and no interest is charged. Miss it and Mississippi Code 27-41-9 adds interest of one-half of one percent for every month the bill sits unpaid.

  • January 1: assessment date and ownership date.
  • April 1: deadline for homestead exemption, builder affidavits and business personal property renditions.
  • First Monday in July: the assessment rolls are presented.
  • First Monday in August: the Board of Supervisors starts hearing appeals.
  • February 1: payment due date.

A closing that falls near any of these dates needs a little planning. Decide in the purchase contract who covers the February 1 bill, then ask the title company to show that split on the settlement statement so nobody argues about it later. If you are listing in spring, mention the April 1 homestead deadline to your buyer too, since a missed filing means a full-rate bill.

How hurricanes affect taxes and house sales

Storms are part of this county's property record. Hurricane Camille hit in August 1969 and Hurricane Katrina on August 29, 2005, and both did catastrophic damage along the coast.

State law builds in some relief for payment delays. Under Mississippi Code 27-41-9, the governor may extend the date for charging interest by proclamation when unusual conditions delay payment through no fault of the taxpayer or the collector. The extension can run up to 60 days, with two more extensions possible. The state tax agency has also published guidance on possible relief under section 27-35-143(9), which lets boards of supervisors adjust assessments in certain circumstances. Ask the chancery clerk whether that section applies to your parcel.

Unrepaired roof or water damage lowers a house's value and can block a buyer's financing, because a lender's inspector may refuse to sign off. That is why owners here sometimes sell as-is. If you think storm damage should lower your assessment, the appeal window closes on the first Monday in August.

Why neighbors can pay different amounts

Four public school districts divide the county. The Jackson County School District covers Hurley, Wade, Big Point, Three Rivers, Harleston, Vestry, Latimer and Vancleave, plus St. Martin and a small part of Escatawpa. Pascagoula-Gautier serves Pascagoula and most of Gautier, Moss Point serves Moss Point and most of Escatawpa, and Ocean Springs serves Ocean Springs.

The county, each city and each school district set their own levy, and they add together into one millage rate. A house worth the same money can carry a bigger or smaller bill depending on which side of a district line it sits. Find out your district before quoting a tax figure to a buyer.

What happens to unpaid Jackson County taxes?

Unpaid real estate tax puts the property in line for the county tax auction. The state permits these sales on the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August. The collector's office can tell you which date this county uses.

Losing the sale does not end your claim right away. The former owner has two years counted from the sale date to buy the property back, paying the overdue taxes along with statutory damages and interest, and the chancery clerk is supposed to send notice of that right. Only if the two years run out does the buyer become eligible for a tax deed. For land sold to the state, the Secretary of State can be reached at 1-866-835-2637.

Selling with taxes, liens or storm damage

Owing back taxes does not stop a sale. A title search finds the balance and the closing agent pays it from your proceeds, the same way a lien or a leftover mortgage balance is paid.

  1. Get a written payoff number for any past-due taxes from the collector before you list or say yes to an offer.
  2. Confirm your homestead status. A single-family home you live in is assessed at 10 percent of value rather than 15 percent, and you apply between January 1 and April 1.
  3. Collect insurance and repair records if the house had flood or wind damage.
  4. Have an attorney or title company draw up the deed.
  5. On closing day the payoffs come out of what you are owed, the buyer signs, and the title company sends the new deed for recording.

With no lender in the picture, a cash purchase can close faster on a house that would fail a financing inspection. Cash Home Buyers looks at each Jackson County property individually and does not set a price or a timeline until we have the details.

Frequently asked questions

Is Jackson County, MS the same as Jackson, MS?

No. Jackson County is on the Mississippi Gulf Coast with Pascagoula as its seat, about 190 miles from the city of Jackson, which is in Hinds County. Each place has its own property tax office.

When are property taxes due in Jackson County, Mississippi?

By February 1 each year. A weekend or holiday deadline slides to Monday with no interest. After that, interest builds at one-half of one percent each month.

Where do I pay Jackson County property tax?

Pay the Tax Collector at 2915 Canty Street in Pascagoula, or mail it to Box 998, Pascagoula, MS 39568. The phone is 228-769-3074, and the office is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays.

How do I appeal a Jackson County assessment?

Ask the Chancery Clerk to set a hearing before the Board of Supervisors. File by the first Monday in August, the day hearings begin.

Can I sell a Jackson County, MS house after hurricane damage?

Yes. Buyers who accept the repairs will take a damaged house as-is. Taxes owed come out of the proceeds, and the title company checks for liens first.

Rankin County in brief

Rankin County lies in central Mississippi along the Pearl River, right beside Hinds County and the Jackson area. Brandon is the county seat. The 2020 count was 157,031 residents, and a five-member board of supervisors serves four-year terms.

The county grew from a mostly farm economy into a suburban one over the twentieth century, and the population went from almost 44,000 in 1970 to more than 69,000 a decade later. That growth explains the mix a seller meets today: newer subdivisions close to Jackson, older houses in the small towns and rural lots on the edges.

Offices that handle taxes and land records

Three offices matter when you sell: the Tax Assessor, the Tax Collector and the Chancery Clerk. Payments go to the Tax Collector. The other two are below.

Expect to phone all three offices. The Tax Collector tells you what is owed this year, the Tax Assessor tells you whether homestead is on file and how the parcel is valued, and the Chancery Clerk tells you who holds title and whether the land has any sale or redemption history. Writing down each answer with the date of the call gives your title company something solid to work from.

The clerk's office runs separate pages for e-recording, recording requirements and delinquent taxes. Under state law the clerk is the custodian of land records and also runs the annual county tax sale, as the Department of Revenue explains.

Homestead exemption

File with the Rankin County Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1. The first filing has to be made in person, and the county's Filings and Exemptions page explains that the benefit then renews each year unless your filing status changes.

A fresh application is required after any of these:

  • A change in ownership, use or occupancy.
  • Acquiring new property or a change in the property description.
  • Turning sixty-five or becoming 100% disabled for the first time.

The county warns that failing to report a homestead change can mean a fine of up to $5,000, two years in prison, or both. An owner who is 65 or older, or 100% disabled, is generally exempt on 160 acres or about $75,000 of appraised value, whichever limit comes first, and the rest is taxed.

Selling counts as a change in ownership, so tell the Tax Assessor once the deed is recorded. Doing it promptly keeps the exemption record clean and protects you from the fine described above.

How taxes are figured and what happens if they are late

Bills follow the state formula: true value, times the assessment ratio, times the combined millage for your county, your school district and, inside a city, that city. Classification works like this: a home occupied by its owner is rated at 10% of true value and everything else at 15%, as the Department of Revenue FAQ lays out.

The due date is February 1. A parcel left unpaid can go to the county tax auction. Depending on the county, that sale is the first Monday of April or the last Monday of August, and Rankin's own page is where to confirm which.

Once a sale has happened, the Chancery Clerk's Land Redemption page has an online search for delinquent tax amounts and redemption details. Credit card payments carry a 2.5% convenience charge, and debit transactions a $2.25 flat fee. Call the clerk at 601-825-1469 with questions.

A seller who is behind should find the exact amount before listing instead of waiting. Closing stalls until that figure is known, and having it lets you choose between paying now and letting the sale absorb it.

Recording a deed in Rankin County

The recorder can add $10 when a document does not follow the format rules in Miss. Code 89-5-24. Fees can change, which is why a short call to the Rankin Chancery Clerk beats guessing at a check amount. Our Mississippi quitclaim deed guide covers format and recording rules in more detail.

What sellers in Rankin County usually face

Three situations account for most Rankin sales that need a little extra care: back taxes, an inherited house, and a place with repairs a buyer's lender would object to. Pulling records together early helps in all three.

  • Ask the Chancery Clerk to confirm the deed of record and any tax sale or redemption history.
  • If the house is inherited, learn whether an estate is open and read our probate guide.
  • Watch the county website for posted notices before you plan yard clearing or burning.

A typical sale runs in order: confirm who owns the house and what is owed, sign a contract, let the title company search and clear the title, then close and record the deed with the Chancery Clerk. Anything owed to the county is paid out of your proceeds at the closing table.

Before the first call, put your papers in one place. Bring your deed, your newest tax statement and any mortgage payoff letter, plus the lease if the house is rented. If the house passed through an estate, add the court papers. Having these in one folder lets a title company or a buyer answer ownership questions in a single call instead of several.

Calendar dates deserve a look too. Homestead filings close April 1, the bill is due February 1, and the auction lands in April or August. A sale scheduled to close ahead of the auction date lets the title company pay the county before any buyer can bid, which keeps the tax-deed clock from ever starting.

Lafayette County in brief

North Mississippi's Lafayette County has Oxford as its seat and its largest town. The 2020 count was 55,813 residents. The University of Mississippi is inside the county, which shapes the housing market: student rentals, game-day visitors and faculty buyers all show up in local sales. Abbeville and Taylor are the other incorporated towns, and the Lafayette County and Oxford school districts split the public schools.

With so many houses rented to students, plenty of sellers are landlords. Others are heirs of long-held family property in the smaller communities such as Yocona, Springdale or Denmark.

Who handles property tax

One elected official, the Tax Assessor/Collector, does both jobs here. The office is at 300 N. Lamar Blvd., Suite 103, in Oxford. Call 662-234-6006 for the collector side or 662-234-5562 for the assessor side. The fax number is 662-238-7992.

The office takes cash, credit cards and money orders, and it takes a personal check if you show a driver's license and leave a phone number. Links are on the Tax Assessor/Collector page. The assessor sets values only, and other bodies set the rate.

Oxford's city website also links to an online property tax payment page. Ask whether a house inside the city limits gets a separate city bill before you assume the county bill is the only one.

How to appeal your assessment

Start informally at the assessor's office, then go formal with the Board of Supervisors if you still disagree. The informal meeting is only a review. Staff pull your property record card, explain how the value was reached, compare your house with similar ones and screen you for exemptions.

A formal appeal starts when you contact the Chancery Clerk at P.O. Box 1240, Oxford, MS 38655 and send a copy to the Tax Collector/Assessor. The county says appeals are stronger when they show comparable properties assessed for less, and it calls a recent appraisal of your own property the best evidence.

At the hearing the board looks at fairness and accuracy. Whether you can afford the bill is not part of the hearing. Foreclosures, short sales, bankruptcy sales, auctions and bank-owned homes are not treated as good sales when true values are set, so a discounted sale next door will not pull your value down.

  • First Monday in July: real and personal property rolls are presented.
  • July: rolls are open to the public.
  • First Monday in August: filing deadline for the Board of Supervisors.
  • Third Monday in August: values and appeals are finalized.

Book your informal review in July while the rolls are open, so you still have time to file formally by the August deadline.

Homestead exemption

Homestead gives the home you live in a lower assessment ratio. Live in your own single-family house and it is assessed at 10 percent of appraised value, not 15. File with the assessor from January 1 to April 1.

Once approved, you stay on the list unless your status changes. Miss April 1 and you lose the exemption for that assessment year. If you are 65 or older, or totally disabled, and otherwise qualify, the first $75,000 of true value is exempt. Eligibility can be lost by not complying with state income tax law or by tagging a car in another county.

Homestead follows the owner, not the house, and that shows up at closing. A buyer who plans to rent the place out may land at the higher ratio. Ask the assessor how a change of ownership is treated before you guess at next year's bill.

How the Lafayette County tax sale works

Oxford-area parcels that stay delinquent go to an online auction at GovEase.com. It starts the last Monday of August and runs 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. daily until every parcel has sold. Bidders register for free and need a Social Security or Tax ID number, a W-9, a way to pay and a maximum bid. The parcels are advertised twice in August in The Oxford Eagle.

By law, overbids go to the county general fund. An owner who redeems pays the original starting amount plus interest. Once two years pass from the purchase date without redemption, the buyer can claim the property by tax deed. Land forfeited to the state can be bought through the Public Lands Division at 601-359-6373, or toll free in Mississippi at 1-866-TFLANDS.

For an owner who is behind, the two-year clock starts at the sale, not when the bill goes late. Close your own sale before the last Monday in August and the title company can pay the taxes at the table.

Common seller situations in Oxford and the county

Four situations come up again and again:

  • Student rentals: a lease may run past the planned closing date, so read it before you set a closing day.
  • Inherited homes: probate runs through the chancery court, and the Chancery Clerk's office is where heirs begin.
  • Delinquent taxes: ask the Tax Collector/Assessor for a payoff figure, and the closing pays it off.
  • Value disputes: the informal review and the August appeal date apply to your parcel whether you plan to sell or stay.

A cash purchase moves faster than a financed one when a property needs work or when the heirs live in different states. Cash Home Buyers evaluates each Lafayette County house individually and does not quote a price or a date before reviewing it.

Recording the deed

The Chancery Clerk records deeds and keeps the land records. The sequence runs from a title search by an attorney or title company, to a deed carrying the seller's notarized signature, a legal description and both parties' details, to recording. Ask the Lafayette clerk whether any local requirement differs.

Since ownership for assessment is fixed as of January 1, spell out in the contract who pays the February 1 bill, and have the title company document that.

How a bill is figured and what late payment costs

The state formula multiplies true value by the assessment ratio and then by the millage rate. The county, a municipality and the school district each set their own levy, and the three add together. A bill still open after February 1 picks up interest of one-half of one percent for each month or part of a month, under Mississippi Code 27-41-9.

Frequently asked questions

Yes. The title search will list back taxes, and closing pays them out of your proceeds. A house already sold at auction can still be redeemed by the owner within two years.

Assessor and Collector in downtown Hattiesburg

Both county tax offices sit at 601 N. Main Street, Hattiesburg. Each year the assessor must locate, classify and value all taxable property, which comes to about 50,000 real and personal parcels.

  • Assessor: (601) 545-6130, mail to P.O. Box 1626, Hattiesburg, MS 39403.
  • Collector: (601) 582-8228, with statements also handled through P.O. Box 1689, Hattiesburg, MS 39403.
  • Parcels appear on TSC Maps, which shows ownership, values, aerial views and legal descriptions.
  • The state requires new aerial photography every ten years, and Forrest County had new photos flown in early 2022.

State rules call for a new valuation of real property every four years at minimum. Finished rolls go before the Board of Supervisors, and residents may look them over and protest before approval by the board and the state.

How a Forrest County bill is figured

Three numbers produce the bill: the true value of the property, the ratio tied to its class, and the millage from the taxing bodies. The Board of Supervisors, Hattiesburg and Petal each add a levy. A single-family home its owner lives in is Class I, taxed at 10% of true value. Class II covers other real property at 15%, Class III personal property at 15%, Class IV public utilities at 30% and Class V motor vehicles at 30%.

For an official millage figure, use the combined county and city schedules on the Department of Revenue property tax data page.

The city of Hattiesburg crosses the line into Lamar County. Two houses a mile apart on the west side may therefore answer to different assessors, collectors and millage. Before you tell a buyer what the monthly cost looks like, ask the Forrest County Tax Collector which districts cover your parcel. The county also has three school systems, and Petal and Hattiesburg addresses go to different ones.

Due dates and a freshly recorded deed

Payment is due by February 1 for the property assessed the year before, with a weekend or holiday pushing it to the next Monday. Sellers should know about a delay in the county roll: mapping staff handle the prior year's deeds, so a new owner's name can take up to a year to appear.

The result is that a buyer may be mailed a bill under the seller's name, and a seller may still get statements after closing. Whoever signs the settlement statement should hand the Tax Collector a new mailing address. The office asks for every change of address or mortgage status. Statements go either to the mortgage company or to individuals on the mailing list.

Mobile and manufactured homes follow a separate schedule. Register one within seven days of buying it, and expect the first tax due within 90 days and annually after that. An owner can pay a fee to declare a mobile home as real property, which changes how it is assessed.

How to contest an assessment

Begin with a conversation at the assessor's counter. Repair bids and photographs help if you think a value is wrong. The next step is a hearing request to the Board of Supervisors, made through the Chancery Clerk, and it normally has to be on file by the first Monday in August, ahead of the due date.

Protests are accepted once the rolls are compiled and before the board signs off. Call the assessor to learn when that window opens this year, and write down who you spoke with and what you were told.

What happens if taxes go unpaid?

Real estate with unpaid tax may be put up at the county tax sale. Depending on the county, that is held the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August.

  • Redemption by the landowner stays open for two years after the sale (Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3).
  • If no one bids, the State takes the land and the Secretary of State manages it.
  • Business personal property carries its own rendition, due April 1, and missing it brings a mandatory 10% penalty.

Selling in Hattiesburg and Petal

Local sellers usually fret over closing timing, a roll that trails a fresh deed, and repair items a lender may flag. A cash buyer takes the house as-is, so repairs do not hold up closing. Liens and unpaid taxes still have to be cleared through title.

Before listing or accepting an offer, collect the deed, the latest tax statement and any homestead paperwork. Phone the Tax Collector at (601) 582-8228 to confirm the amount owed, then ask the title company to put the payoff on the closing statement. A parcel sold at a tax sale adds the redemption amount to that list. The 2025 population estimate was 79,034, up from 78,158 in 2020.

A checklist before you sign a sale contract

  1. Find the deed and the newest tax statement, and read the owner name and mailing address on the statement.
  2. Call the Collector and ask for the current balance and any earlier-year balance on the parcel.
  3. Check whether homestead is on the account. If you are leaving, plan to tell the buyer that a new filing is needed before April 1.
  4. Look up the parcel on TSC Maps and compare the legal description and acreage with your deed.
  5. Tell the title company about any mobile home on the lot, since it follows its own registration and tax timeline.
  6. After closing, report the change of address so statements stop going to the wrong person.

None of this takes long, and doing it before you list means a buyer's agent hears clear answers when they ask about taxes. A cash buyer will often move on a short timeline, so having these papers in one place keeps the sale from stalling at the last step.

The county at a glance

This Pine Belt county in southeast Mississippi has Hattiesburg as its seat and largest city, with Petal as the second. Interstate 59 and U.S. 11, 49 and 98 cross it. De Soto National Forest covers part of the county, and rural land is valued by soil type and productivity rather than like a city lot.

Downtown Hattiesburg at 601 N. Main Street. Call (601) 582-8228 for the Collector, or (601) 545-6130 for the Assessor at the same address.

January 2 through April 1. Filing once is enough unless your circumstances change, and rentals do not qualify.

It can take as long as a year, since mapping staff handle recorded deeds a year behind when they build the current land roll.

Tax office, Supervisors and Chancery Clerk

One office does both tax jobs in Hancock County, and the County Administrator holds the Tax Assessor and Collector role too. It operates from 854 Highway 90, Bay St. Louis, phone (228) 466-5791. A Tax Assessor page on the county site links to tax and fee details and a homestead exemption page.

  • Chancery Clerk and land records: 854 Highway 90, Suite B, phone (228) 467-5404.
  • Assessment appeals are heard by the Board of Supervisors, and the Chancery Clerk is who you call.

Phone ahead before paying or mailing a check, and ask about hours and accepted payment types.

Tax rates and property classes

Five constitutional classes sort Mississippi property, and each county follows them. The tax is true value, times the class ratio, times millage. Levies come separately from the county, each city and the school district, so a Diamondhead house and a house in unincorporated Kiln can carry different totals.

For an official millage number, the Department of Revenue property tax data page lists combined county and city rates for 2012 through 2025. The assessor revalues real property at least once in four years and need not step inside your house.

Due dates and unpaid tax

The person holding the parcel on January 1 owes that year's tax, with payment due February 1. Statements arrive in November and December. A weekend or holiday on the due date gives you until the next Monday with no penalty.

Real property that stays delinquent may be sold at the county tax sale, and the former owner can buy it back within two years (Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3). If nobody bids, the State takes the parcel, and the Secretary of State handles it at 1-866-835-2637.

Get a current payoff, and any earlier-year balance, before you agree to a contract. A title company will not close over delinquent tax, so find out first and price the house afterward.

Contesting an assessment

Disagree with a value? Hearing requests go to the Board of Supervisors by way of the Chancery Clerk. The filing deadline is the first Monday in August, well before the bill, so waiting for the December statement is too late.

Gather proof. Photograph a storm-damaged roof, and note any wrong square footage on the record. When an appraisal used inaccurate information about the size of a home, a refund of earlier years may be possible, and the Chancery Clerk can walk you through it.

Homestead exemption and age rules

A new occupant has to apply for homestead in their own name, so a seller should not expect the exemption to carry over. Applications go to the Tax Assessor from January 1 to April 1, and one filing normally stands until your status changes.

Owners 65 or older, and totally disabled owners who otherwise qualify, owe nothing on the first $75,000 of true value. Two things end eligibility: an owner or spouse out of compliance on state income tax, and a vehicle tagged in another county. Once you have moved out, stop claiming homestead on the old house.

Storm history and flood questions

Hurricane Katrina came ashore here for its final landfall on August 29, 2005, and buyers still ask how a house fared. The storm destroyed nearly the entire first block off the beach, and homes as far as 10 miles inland flooded. Highway 603 south of Interstate 10 was submerged and the Highway 90 bridge at Bay St. Louis was wrecked. Bay St. Louis, Waveland, Pearlington, Diamondhead and Kiln all took heavy damage.

  • A buyer's insurer and lender will ask about flood zone and elevation, and a house with past water damage can be hard to finance.

Selling a Hancock County house

Your house may have storm or flood history, may be inherited, or may have sat empty. Each case calls for its own paperwork.

  2. Request any earlier-year balance from the Tax Assessor and Collector.
  3. Ask the Chancery Clerk whether a tax sale is recorded on the parcel.
  4. Collect repair and insurance records so a buyer can price the house fairly.

With a cash sale the buyer accepts the house as it stands. Clear title and settled current-year tax on the closing statement are still required. Verify each figure with the county office before relying on it.

Steps to take before you list

Your first stop is the combined tax office on Highway 90, where you can ask for the parcel's balance and whether any earlier year is open. Inherited the house? Check that the roll carries the right owner, since a bill addressed to a deceased relative is still owed. Next, the Chancery Clerk's suite in that same building can confirm that no tax sale is recorded and that your deed is on file.

With those answers in hand, think about condition. Buyers and their insurers ask about flood zone and any water damage, so dig out repair receipts and insurance papers early. A cash buyer can overlook cosmetic problems, but the title still has to be clear and the tax record settled. Finally, ask the title company to add the payoff to the closing statement so the county is paid out of your proceeds and nothing follows you after the sale.

Where Hancock County is

Hancock County sits on the Gulf of Mexico at the Louisiana line, and its county seat is Bay St. Louis. It covers 553 square miles, and 79 of them (14%) are water, so much of the county is bayou, bay and marsh. The 2020 census counted 46,053 people.

The three cities are Bay St. Louis, Diamondhead and Waveland. Kiln and Pearlington are census-designated places, and smaller communities include Lakeshore, Clermont Harbor, Necaise and Napoleon. The John C. Stennis Space Center is in the county, which is part of the Gulfport-Biloxi metropolitan area. I-10, U.S. 90 and MS 43, 53, 603 and 607 are the major routes. Three school districts operate here, Bay St. Louis, Hancock County and Picayune, so check which one your address falls in.
